system.description:
Gramuz

Les Gramuz, dont le nom signifie « Hommes des Plaines » dans leur langue, descendent d’anciens Eriadoriens qui franchirent la Trouée de l’Isen au début du Troisième Âge avant de gagner les vastes plaines du Rhovanion. Ils s’établirent principalement au nord du Nan Celduin, la vallée du Celduin, dans des régions de collines douces, de pâturages ouverts et de terres fertiles parcourues par de nombreux cours d’eau. Leur culture est profondément rurale, fondée sur la famille, le clan, l’élevage et le travail de la terre.

Origines

Les Gramuz sont généralement de taille moyenne à grande, avec une silhouette robuste et parfois trapue. Les hommes atteignent souvent environ un mètre quatre-vingt-trois et les femmes un mètre soixante-trois. Leur teint est clair, leurs cheveux le plus souvent blonds et leurs yeux fréquemment bleus. Leur espérance de vie se situe généralement entre soixante-cinq et quatre-vingt-cinq ans.

Apparence

Les hommes portent volontiers la barbe, qui constitue souvent un signe de maturité, de respectabilité et d’appartenance familiale. Les coiffures et les vêtements restent simples, mais les familles aisées peuvent utiliser des broderies, des fibules ou des ceintures ouvragées pour afficher leur rang.

Communautés

La société gramuz est essentiellement agraire. La plupart des familles vivent dans de petites communautés dispersées, composées d’une à trois maisonnées apparentées. Ces établissements ne forment pas toujours de véritables villages : il s’agit plutôt de groupes de fermes installées à proximité d’un refuge commun.

Clans et chefs

Les habitations rappellent les longues maisons des autres Hommes du Nord, mais en version plus courte et plus adaptée à la vie de petits groupes familiaux. Elles réunissent souvent sous un même toit les membres de la famille, les réserves et parfois certains animaux durant les mois les plus froids.

Famille

Chaque communauté dispose généralement d’un lieu défendable : une colline entourée d’une palissade, un enclos protégé par un fossé, une petite motte fortifiée ou un refuge proche d’un gué ou d’un bosquet. En temps de paix, ces espaces servent surtout à rassembler les animaux domestiques. En cas de raid ou d’attaque, ils deviennent le cœur de la défense collective.

Agriculture et élevage

Les Gramuz sont organisés en clans dirigés par des chefs héréditaires. L’autorité de ces derniers repose sur leur lignée, mais aussi sur leur capacité à protéger les terres, arbitrer les querelles et redistribuer les ressources lors des périodes difficiles.

Fêtes

Le chef n’est pas un souverain absolu. Il doit tenir compte des anciens, des chefs de famille et de la réputation des guerriers les plus respectés. Une décision contraire aux intérêts du clan peut être contestée, surtout si elle menace les troupeaux, les récoltes ou l’honneur collectif.

Religion

Les Gramuz sont indépendants et déterminés. Ils acceptent difficilement une autorité étrangère lorsqu’elle ne repose ni sur la parenté ni sur un serment reconnu. Cette indépendance ne les empêche pas de conclure des alliances, mais ils exigent généralement des accords clairs et personnels.

Langues

Le mariage est monogame, et la filiation suit traditionnellement la lignée masculine. L’épouse rejoint habituellement la famille de son mari et participe à la maisonnée de celui-ci.

Tempérament

Les unions peuvent être conclues en dehors du clan ou de la tribu, mais les mariages avec des peuples non nordiques restent rares. Cette réserve ne provient pas nécessairement d’une hostilité ouverte : elle tient surtout au désir de préserver les coutumes, les liens de parenté et la cohésion des communautés.

Vêtements

La famille élargie constitue l’unité fondamentale de la société. Les terres, les troupeaux, les outils et les devoirs se transmettent entre générations. Un individu qui perd sa famille se retrouve donc privé non seulement de proches, mais aussi de sa place sociale et économique.

Guerre

Les Gramuz cultivent les céréales, élèvent porcs, bovins, moutons et chevaux, et exploitent les terres riches des vallées fluviales. Leur richesse se mesure moins en pièces de monnaie qu’en bétail, en terres, en réserves et en réputation.

Relations

Le cheval occupe une place importante, sans toutefois dominer toute leur culture comme chez les Rohirrim. Les Gramuz élèvent des montures robustes, adaptées aux travaux agricoles, aux déplacements et à la guerre. Les familles les plus prospères possèdent souvent de bons reproducteurs et peuvent tirer un prestige considérable de la qualité de leurs bêtes.

Professions

Le commerce utilise volontiers la monnaie du Gondor, mais les échanges en nature restent courants. Les animaux, les outils, les céréales, les tissus et les services peuvent tous servir de paiement.

Place dans la création de personnage

Le cycle de l’année structure profondément leur vie. Quatre grandes fêtes réunissent les communautés dispersées : le milieu de l’été, le milieu de l’hiver, l’équinoxe de printemps et l’équinoxe d’automne.

Compléments 16

Ces rassemblements célèbrent le changement des saisons, l’achèvement des travaux et la continuité du clan. Ils permettent également de conclure des mariages, d’échanger des nouvelles, de régler des différends et de renouveler les alliances.

Compléments 17

Les festivités comprennent de grands repas, des jeux d’argent, des concours d’adresse, des épreuves de force, des courses, de la musique et des danses. Les nuits de fête sont souvent bruyantes, chaleureuses et marquées par une consommation généreuse de nourriture et de boisson.

Compléments 18

Le culte de la Terre occupe la place principale dans leur spiritualité. Il honore la fertilité du sol, la stabilité des saisons, les récoltes et la prospérité du foyer.

Compléments 19

Dans certaines régions, le culte de la Croissance est également répandu. Il met davantage l’accent sur la germination, la naissance, le renouveau et l’abondance des troupeaux.

Compléments 20

Ces cultes sont étroitement liés à la vie quotidienne. Les rites peuvent accompagner les semailles, les moissons, la naissance des animaux, l’ouverture d’une nouvelle ferme, les mariages et les fêtes saisonnières.

Compléments 21

La religion gramuz ne repose pas sur un clergé puissant. Elle est transmise par les anciens, les chefs de famille et quelques individus considérés comme particulièrement proches des forces naturelles.

Compléments 22

Les rares utilisateurs de magie appartiennent le plus souvent aux Urdharkona, ou Urdharkonur au pluriel, des spécialistes proches des Animistes. Ils agissent comme guérisseurs, conseillers, interprètes des signes naturels et gardiens des traditions.

Compléments 23

Le gramuik est leur langue principale. Le westron est également connu, surtout dans les communautés proches des routes commerciales ou en contact avec le Gondor.

Compléments 24

Les Gramuz peuvent aussi apprendre le logathig, l’eothrik, l’atliduk, le nahaiduk, le bethteur, certaines formes d’orquien ou de waildyth chez les voyageurs, guerriers et éclaireurs.

Compléments 25

Les Gramuz sont réputés indépendants, déterminés et directs. Ils apprécient les personnes capables de tenir leur parole, de travailler dur et de défendre leurs intérêts sans détour.

Compléments 26

Ils respectent la réussite matérielle lorsqu’elle repose sur l’effort, la prudence et une bonne gestion. Un propriétaire capable d’agrandir ses terres, d’améliorer son troupeau ou de protéger sa communauté gagne naturellement en prestige.

Compléments 27

Cette valorisation de la réussite peut toutefois produire de fortes rivalités. Les querelles portant sur les pâturages, les frontières, les chevaux ou les mariages peuvent durer plusieurs générations lorsqu’aucune autorité reconnue ne parvient à les régler.

Compléments 28

Les Gramuz portent surtout des vêtements de lin et de laine. Leur tenue quotidienne comprend généralement des braies, une tunique ou chemise de longueur moyenne, des jambières, une cape de tissu et des chaussures souples. Les femmes portent souvent une tunique courte ou une robe simple accompagnée de jambières.

Compléments 29

Les Gramuz ne sont pas un peuple exclusivement guerrier, mais presque chaque communauté doit savoir se défendre contre les raids, les Orcs et les bêtes sauvages.

Compléments 30

Leurs armes les plus courantes sont la lance, l’arc court, l’arc long, la hache à une main, l’épée courte et l’épée large. Le cuir est leur protection la plus fréquente. Les guerriers plus riches ou les hommes de la suite d’un chef peuvent porter de la maille ou des armures d’écailles.

Compléments 31

Les Gramuz combattent surtout à pied ou à cheval en petites unités. Ils excellent dans la défense des fermes, les escarmouches, les embuscades et les combats livrés en terrain ouvert.

Compléments 32

Ils haïssent les Orcs, qu’ils considèrent comme des pillards, des meurtriers et des ennemis naturels de leurs communautés. Leurs relations avec les autres Hommes du Nord sont variables. Ils peuvent commercer, s’allier ou se quereller avec les Hommes des Bois, les Éothéod, les Rohirrim ou les communautés urbaines du Rhovanion.

Compléments 33

Ils entretiennent également des rapports économiques avec le Gondor, dont les monnaies circulent dans leurs terres. Certains clans voient favorablement cette influence ; d’autres craignent qu’elle n’affaiblisse leur indépendance.

Compléments 34

Les Gramuz peuvent suivre presque toutes les professions, à l’exception du Barbare et des professions propres à d’autres races ou cultures. Les utilisateurs de magie demeurent rares, et les traditions naturelles des Urdharkona sont les plus courantes parmi eux.

Compléments 35

Leur formation favorise la conduite et le soin des animaux, l’élevage, l’agriculture, la survie dans les plaines, l’observation du temps, le pistage, la cueillette, la cuisine, le travail du cuir et du bois, les armes de chasse et de guerre, la danse et les festivités communautaires.

Compléments 36

Cette Culture convient particulièrement aux personnages issus d’une ferme isolée du Rhovanion, d’un clan d’éleveurs, d’une communauté agricole fortifiée, d’une famille de propriétaires terriens, de la suite d’un chef local, d’un groupe de gardiens de troupeaux ou d’une lignée de marchands de chevaux.

Compléments 37

Les Gramuz sont ainsi un peuple de propriétaires, d’agriculteurs et d’éleveurs farouchement attachés à leurs terres. Leur force ne vient ni de grandes cités ni d’armées permanentes, mais de la cohésion des familles, de leur connaissance des plaines et de leur détermination à préserver les fermes et les troupeaux dont dépend toute leur existence.

Langues de départ

  • Westron — Parlée 6 / Écrite 4

Gramuz

The Gramuz, whose name means “Men of the Plains” in their language, descend from ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Gap of Rohan at the beginning of the Third Age before moving into the vast plains of Rhovanion. They settled chiefly north of Nan Celduin, the valley of the Celduin, in regions of gentle hills, open pasture, and fertile land crossed by many streams. Their culture is profoundly rural, founded on family, clan, animal husbandry, and working the land.

Origins

Gramuz are generally of medium to tall stature, with robust and sometimes stocky builds. Men often reach about six feet and women about five feet four inches. Their complexion is fair, their hair most often blond, and their eyes frequently blue. Their life expectancy generally lies between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Appearance

Men readily wear beards, which often serve as a sign of maturity, respectability, and family belonging. Hairstyles and clothing remain simple, but prosperous families may use embroidery, brooches, or worked belts to display rank.

Communities

Gramuz society is essentially agrarian. Most families live in small, scattered communities made up of one to three related households. These settlements do not always form true villages: they are more often groups of farms established near a common refuge.

Clans and chiefs

Dwellings resemble the longhouses of other Northmen, but in a shorter form better suited to small family groups. Under a single roof they often bring together family members, stores, and sometimes certain animals during the coldest months.

Family

Each community generally has a defensible place: a hill enclosed by a palisade, an enclosure protected by a ditch, a small fortified mound, or a refuge near a ford or grove. In peacetime these spaces are used mainly to gather domestic animals. In the event of raid or attack, they become the heart of collective defense.

Agriculture and animal husbandry

The Gramuz are organized into clans led by hereditary chiefs. The authority of these leaders rests on lineage, but also on their ability to protect the lands, arbitrate disputes, and redistribute resources during difficult periods.

Festivals

The chief is not an absolute ruler. He must take account of elders, heads of households, and the reputation of the most respected warriors. A decision contrary to the clan's interests may be challenged, especially if it threatens herds, crops, or collective honor.

Religion

The Gramuz are independent and determined. They have difficulty accepting foreign authority when it rests neither on kinship nor on a recognized oath. This independence does not prevent alliances, but they generally demand clear and personal agreements.

Languages

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. A wife usually joins her husband's family and becomes part of his household.

Temperament

Unions may be contracted outside the clan or tribe, but marriages with non-Northern peoples remain rare. This reserve does not necessarily arise from open hostility; it mainly reflects a desire to preserve customs, kinship ties, and community cohesion.

Clothing

The extended family is the fundamental unit of society. Land, herds, tools, and duties pass between generations. An individual who loses his family therefore loses not only relatives, but also his social and economic place.

War

The Gramuz cultivate grain, raise pigs, cattle, sheep, and horses, and exploit the rich lands of the river valleys. Their wealth is measured less in coin than in livestock, land, stores, and reputation.

Relations

The horse holds an important place without dominating their entire culture as it does among the Rohirrim. Gramuz breed sturdy mounts suited to farm work, travel, and war. The most prosperous families often own good breeding stock and can gain considerable prestige from the quality of their animals.

Professions

Trade readily uses Gondorian coinage, but exchange in kind remains common. Animals, tools, grain, cloth, and services can all serve as payment.

Place in character creation

The cycle of the year profoundly structures their life. Four great festivals bring scattered communities together: midsummer, midwinter, the spring equinox, and the autumn equinox.

Additional notes 16

These gatherings celebrate the changing seasons, completion of work, and continuity of the clan. They also make it possible to arrange marriages, exchange news, settle disputes, and renew alliances.

Additional notes 17

Festivities include great meals, gambling, contests of skill, feats of strength, races, music, and dancing. Festival nights are often noisy, warm, and marked by generous consumption of food and drink.

Additional notes 18

The Earth Cult holds the foremost place in their spirituality. It honors the fertility of soil, stability of the seasons, harvests, and prosperity of the household.

Additional notes 19

In some regions the Cult of Growth is also widespread. It places greater emphasis on germination, birth, renewal, and abundance of the herds.

Additional notes 20

These cults are closely tied to everyday life. Rites may accompany sowing, harvest, the birth of animals, establishment of a new farm, marriages, and seasonal festivals.

Additional notes 21

Gramuz religion does not rest on a powerful clergy. It is transmitted by elders, heads of households, and a few individuals regarded as especially close to natural forces.

Additional notes 22

The rare spell-users most often belong to the Urdharkona, or Urdharkonur in the plural, specialists close to Animists. They act as healers, advisers, interpreters of natural signs, and guardians of tradition.

Additional notes 23

Gramuik is their principal language. Westron is also known, especially in communities near trade routes or in contact with Gondor.

Additional notes 24

Gramuz may also learn Logathig, Eothrik, Atliduk, Nahaiduk, Bethteur, certain forms of Orcish, or Waildyth among travelers, warriors, and scouts.

Gramuz

Les Gramuz, dont le nom signifie « Hommes des Plaines » dans leur langue, descendent d’anciens Eriadoriens qui franchirent la Trouée de l’Isen au début du Troisième Âge avant de gagner les vastes plaines du Rhovanion. Ils s’établirent principalement au nord du Nan Celduin, la vallée du Celduin, dans des régions de collines douces, de pâturages ouverts et de terres fertiles parcourues par de nombreux cours d’eau. Leur culture est profondément rurale, fondée sur la famille, le clan, l’élevage et le travail de la terre.

Origines

Les Gramuz sont généralement de taille moyenne à grande, avec une silhouette robuste et parfois trapue. Les hommes atteignent souvent environ un mètre quatre-vingt-trois et les femmes un mètre soixante-trois. Leur teint est clair, leurs cheveux le plus souvent blonds et leurs yeux fréquemment bleus. Leur espérance de vie se situe généralement entre soixante-cinq et quatre-vingt-cinq ans.

Apparence

Les hommes portent volontiers la barbe, qui constitue souvent un signe de maturité, de respectabilité et d’appartenance familiale. Les coiffures et les vêtements restent simples, mais les familles aisées peuvent utiliser des broderies, des fibules ou des ceintures ouvragées pour afficher leur rang.

Communautés

La société gramuz est essentiellement agraire. La plupart des familles vivent dans de petites communautés dispersées, composées d’une à trois maisonnées apparentées. Ces établissements ne forment pas toujours de véritables villages : il s’agit plutôt de groupes de fermes installées à proximité d’un refuge commun.

Clans et chefs

Les habitations rappellent les longues maisons des autres Hommes du Nord, mais en version plus courte et plus adaptée à la vie de petits groupes familiaux. Elles réunissent souvent sous un même toit les membres de la famille, les réserves et parfois certains animaux durant les mois les plus froids.

Famille

Chaque communauté dispose généralement d’un lieu défendable : une colline entourée d’une palissade, un enclos protégé par un fossé, une petite motte fortifiée ou un refuge proche d’un gué ou d’un bosquet. En temps de paix, ces espaces servent surtout à rassembler les animaux domestiques. En cas de raid ou d’attaque, ils deviennent le cœur de la défense collective.

Agriculture et élevage

Les Gramuz sont organisés en clans dirigés par des chefs héréditaires. L’autorité de ces derniers repose sur leur lignée, mais aussi sur leur capacité à protéger les terres, arbitrer les querelles et redistribuer les ressources lors des périodes difficiles.

Fêtes

Le chef n’est pas un souverain absolu. Il doit tenir compte des anciens, des chefs de famille et de la réputation des guerriers les plus respectés. Une décision contraire aux intérêts du clan peut être contestée, surtout si elle menace les troupeaux, les récoltes ou l’honneur collectif.

Religion

Les Gramuz sont indépendants et déterminés. Ils acceptent difficilement une autorité étrangère lorsqu’elle ne repose ni sur la parenté ni sur un serment reconnu. Cette indépendance ne les empêche pas de conclure des alliances, mais ils exigent généralement des accords clairs et personnels.

Langues

Le mariage est monogame, et la filiation suit traditionnellement la lignée masculine. L’épouse rejoint habituellement la famille de son mari et participe à la maisonnée de celui-ci.

Tempérament

Les unions peuvent être conclues en dehors du clan ou de la tribu, mais les mariages avec des peuples non nordiques restent rares. Cette réserve ne provient pas nécessairement d’une hostilité ouverte : elle tient surtout au désir de préserver les coutumes, les liens de parenté et la cohésion des communautés.

Vêtements

La famille élargie constitue l’unité fondamentale de la société. Les terres, les troupeaux, les outils et les devoirs se transmettent entre générations. Un individu qui perd sa famille se retrouve donc privé non seulement de proches, mais aussi de sa place sociale et économique.

Les Gramuz cultivent les céréales, élèvent porcs, bovins, moutons et chevaux, et exploitent les terres riches des vallées fluviales. Leur richesse se mesure moins en pièces de monnaie qu’en bétail, en terres, en réserves et en réputation.

Les Gramuz élèvent des montures robustes, adaptées aux travaux agricoles, aux déplacements et à la guerre. Les familles les plus prospères possèdent souvent de bons reproducteurs et peuvent tirer un prestige considérable de la qualité de leurs bêtes.

Le commerce utilise volontiers la monnaie du Gondor, mais les échanges en nature restent courants. Les animaux, les outils, les céréales, les tissus et les services peuvent tous servir de paiement.

Le cycle de l’année structure profondément leur vie. Quatre grandes fêtes réunissent les communautés dispersées : le milieu de l’été, le milieu de l’hiver, l’équinoxe de printemps et l’équinoxe d’automne.

Les Gramuz ne sont pas un peuple exclusivement guerrier, mais presque chaque communauté doit savoir se défendre contre les raids, les Orcs et les bêtes sauvages.

Compléments 31

Les Gramuz combattent surtout à pied ou à cheval en petites unités. Ils excellent dans la défense des fermes, les escarmouches, les embuscades et les combats livrés en terrain ouvert.

Compléments 32

Ils haïssent les Orcs, qu’ils considèrent comme des pillards, des meurtriers et des ennemis naturels de leurs communautés. Leurs relations avec les autres Hommes du Nord sont variables. Gramuz

The Gramuz, whose name means “Men of the Plains” in their language, descend from ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Gap of Rohan at the beginning of the Third Age before moving into the vast plains of Rhovanion. They settled chiefly north of Nan Celduin, the valley of the Celduin, in regions of gentle hills, open pasture, and fertile land crossed by many streams. Their culture is profoundly rural, founded on family, clan, animal husbandry, and working the land.

Origins

Gramuz are generally of medium to tall stature, with robust and sometimes stocky builds. Men often reach about six feet and women about five feet four inches. Their complexion is fair, their hair most often blond, and their eyes frequently blue. Their life expectancy generally lies between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Appearance

Men readily wear beards, which often serve as a sign of maturity, respectability, and family belonging. Hairstyles and clothing remain simple, but prosperous families may use embroidery, brooches, or worked belts to display rank.

Communities

Gramuz society is essentially agrarian. Most families live in small, scattered communities made up of one to three related households. These settlements do not always form true villages: they are more often groups of farms established near a common refuge.

Clans and chiefs

Dwellings resemble the longhouses of other Northmen, but in a shorter form better suited to small family groups. Under a single roof they often bring together family members, stores, and sometimes certain animals during the coldest months.

Family

Each community generally has a defensible place: a hill enclosed by a palisade, an enclosure protected by a ditch, a small fortified mound, or a refuge near a ford or grove. In peacetime these spaces are used mainly to gather domestic animals. In the event of raid or attack, they become the heart of collective defense.

Agriculture and animal husbandry

The Gramuz are organized into clans led by hereditary chiefs. The authority of these leaders rests on lineage, but also on their ability to protect the lands, arbitrate disputes, and redistribute resources during difficult periods.

Festivals

The chief is not an absolute ruler. He must take account of elders, heads of households, and the reputation of the most respected warriors. A decision contrary to the clan's interests may be challenged, especially if it threatens herds, crops, or collective honor.

Religion

The Gramuz are independent and determined. They have difficulty accepting foreign authority when it rests neither on kinship nor on a recognized oath. This independence does not prevent alliances, but they generally demand clear and personal agreements.

Languages

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. A wife usually joins her husband's family and becomes part of his household.

Temperament

Unions may be contracted outside the clan or tribe, but marriages with non-Northern peoples remain rare. This reserve does not necessarily arise from open hostility; it mainly reflects a desire to preserve customs, kinship ties, and community cohesion.

Clothing

Les Gramuz sont généralement de taille moyenne à grande, avec une silhouette robuste et parfois trapue. Les hommes atteignent souvent environ un mètre quatre-vingt-trois et les femmes un mètre soixante-trois. Leur teint est clair, leurs cheveux le plus souvent blonds et leurs yeux fréquemment bleus. Leur espérance de vie se situe généralement entre soixante-cinq et quatre-vingt-cinq ans.

Apparence

Les hommes portent volontiers la barbe, qui constitue souvent un signe de maturité, de respectabilité et d’appartenance familiale. Les coiffures et les vêtements restent simples, mais les familles aisées peuvent utiliser des broderies, des fibules ou des ceintures ouvragées pour afficher leur rang.

La société gramuz est essentiellement agraire. La plupart des familles vivent dans de petites communautés dispersées, composées d’une à trois maisonnées apparentées. Ces établissements ne forment pas toujours de véritables villages : il s’agit plutôt de groupes de fermes installées à proximité d’un refuge commun.

Les habitations rappellent les longues maisons des autres Hommes du Nord, mais en version plus courte et plus adaptée à la vie de petits groupes familiaux. The Gramuz, whose name means “Men of the Plains” in their language, descend from ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Gap of Rohan at the beginning of the Third Age before moving into the vast plains of Rhovanion. They settled chiefly north of Nan Celduin, the valley of the Celduin, in regions of gentle hills, open pasture, and fertile land crossed by many streams. Their culture is profoundly rural, founded on family, clan, animal husbandry, and working the land.

Origins

Gramuz are generally of medium to tall stature, with robust and sometimes stocky builds. Men often reach about six feet and women about five feet four inches. Their complexion is fair, their hair most often blond, and their eyes frequently blue. Their life expectancy generally lies between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Appearance

Men readily wear beards, which often serve as a sign of maturity, respectability, and family belonging. Hairstyles and clothing remain simple, but prosperous families may use embroidery, brooches, or worked belts to display rank.

Communities

Gramuz society is essentially agrarian. Most families live in small, scattered communities made up of one to three related households. These settlements do not always form true villages: they are more often groups of farms established near a common refuge.

Clans and chiefs

Dwellings resemble the longhouses of other Northmen, but in a shorter form better suited to small family groups. Under a single roof they often bring together family members, stores, and sometimes certain animals during the coldest months.

Family

Each community generally has a defensible place: a hill enclosed by a palisade, an enclosure protected by a ditch, a small fortified mound, or a refuge near a ford or grove. Agriculture and animal husbandry

The Gramuz are organized into clans led by hereditary chiefs. The authority of these leaders rests on lineage, but also on their ability to protect the lands, arbitrate disputes, and redistribute resources during difficult periods.

Festivals

The chief is not an absolute ruler. He must take account of elders, heads of households, and the reputation of the most respected warriors. A decision contrary to the clan's interests may be challenged, especially if it threatens herds, crops, or collective honor.

Religion

The Gramuz are independent and determined. They have difficulty accepting foreign authority when it rests neither on kinship nor on a recognized oath. This independence does not prevent alliances, but they generally demand clear and personal agreements.

Languages

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. A wife usually joins her husband's family and becomes part of his household.

Temperament

Unions may be contracted outside the clan or tribe, but marriages with non-Northern peoples remain rare. This reserve does not necessarily arise from open hostility; it mainly reflects a desire to preserve customs, kinship ties, and community cohesion.

Clothing

The extended family is the fundamental unit of society. Land, herds, tools, and duties pass between generations. An individual who loses his family therefore loses not only relatives, but also his social and economic place.

War

The Gramuz cultivate grain, raise pigs, cattle, sheep, and horses, and exploit the rich lands of the river valleys. Their wealth is measured less in coin than in livestock, land, stores, and reputation.

Professions

Trade readily uses Gondorian coinage, but exchange in kind remains common. Animals, tools, grain, cloth, and services can all serve as payment.

The cycle of the year profoundly structures their life. Four great festivals bring scattered communities together: midsummer, midwinter, the spring equinox, and the autumn equinox.

These gatherings celebrate the changing seasons, completion of work, and continuity of the clan. They also make it possible to arrange marriages, exchange news, settle disputes, and renew alliances.

Additional notes 17

Festivities include great meals, gambling, contests of skill, feats of strength, races, music, and dancing. Festival nights are often noisy, warm, and marked by generous consumption of food and drink.

Additional notes 18

Additional notes 19

Additional notes 20

These cults are closely tied to everyday life. Rites may accompany sowing, harvest, the birth of animals, establishment of a new farm, marriages, and seasonal festivals.

Additional notes 21

Additional notes 24

Additional notes 25

Additional notes 26

Additional notes 27

This appreciation of success can nevertheless produce strong rivalries. Disputes over pasture, boundaries, horses, or marriages can last for several generations when no recognized authority succeeds in settling them.

Additional notes 28

Additional notes 29

Additional notes 30

Additional notes 31

Gramuz fight mainly on foot or horseback in small units. They excel at defending farms, skirmishing, ambushes, and battles fought in open terrain.

Additional notes 32

Additional notes 34

Additional notes 35

Additional notes 37

The Gramuz are thus a people of landowners, farmers, and herders fiercely attached to their lands. Gramuz

The Gramuz, whose name means “Men of the Plains” in their language, descend from ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Gap of Rohan at the beginning of the Third Age before moving into the vast plains of Rhovanion. They settled chiefly north of Nan Celduin, the valley of the Celduin, in regions of gentle hills, open pasture, and fertile land crossed by many streams. Their culture is profoundly rural, founded on family, clan, animal husbandry, and working the land.

Origins

Gramuz are generally of medium to tall stature, with robust and sometimes stocky builds. Men often reach about six feet and women about five feet four inches. Their complexion is fair, their hair most often blond, and their eyes frequently blue. Their life expectancy generally lies between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Appearance

Men readily wear beards, which often serve as a sign of maturity, respectability, and family belonging. Hairstyles and clothing remain simple, but prosperous families may use embroidery, brooches, or worked belts to display rank.

Communities

Gramuz society is essentially agrarian. Most families live in small, scattered communities made up of one to three related households. These settlements do not always form true villages: they are more often groups of farms established near a common refuge.

Clans and chiefs

Dwellings resemble the longhouses of other Northmen, but in a shorter form better suited to small family groups. Under a single roof they often bring together family members, stores, and sometimes certain animals during the coldest months.

Family

Each community generally has a defensible place: a hill enclosed by a palisade, an enclosure protected by a ditch, a small fortified mound, or a refuge near a ford or grove. In peacetime these spaces are used mainly to gather domestic animals. In the event of raid or attack, they become the heart of collective defense.

Agriculture and animal husbandry

The Gramuz are organized into clans led by hereditary chiefs. The authority of these leaders rests on lineage, but also on their ability to protect the lands, arbitrate disputes, and redistribute resources during difficult periods.

Festivals

The chief is not an absolute ruler. He must take account of elders, heads of households, and the reputation of the most respected warriors. A decision contrary to the clan's interests may be challenged, especially if it threatens herds, crops, or collective honor.

Religion

The Gramuz are independent and determined. They have difficulty accepting foreign authority when it rests neither on kinship nor on a recognized oath. This independence does not prevent alliances, but they generally demand clear and personal agreements.

Languages

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. A wife usually joins her husband's family and becomes part of his household.

Temperament

Unions may be contracted outside the clan or tribe, but marriages with non-Northern peoples remain rare. This reserve does not necessarily arise from open hostility; it mainly reflects a desire to preserve customs, kinship ties, and community cohesion.

Clothing

The extended family is the fundamental unit of society. Land, herds, tools, and duties pass between generations. An individual who loses his family therefore loses not only relatives, but also his social and economic place.

War

The Gramuz cultivate grain, raise pigs, cattle, sheep, and horses, and exploit the rich lands of the river valleys. Their wealth is measured less in coin than in livestock, land, stores, and reputation.

Relations

The horse holds an important place without dominating their entire culture as it does among the Rohirrim. Gramuz breed sturdy mounts suited to farm work, travel, and war. The most prosperous families often own good breeding stock and can gain considerable prestige from the quality of their animals.

Professions

Trade readily uses Gondorian coinage, but exchange in kind remains common. Animals, tools, grain, cloth, and services can all serve as payment.

Place in character creation

The cycle of the year profoundly structures their life. Four great festivals bring scattered communities together: midsummer, midwinter, the spring equinox, and the autumn equinox.

These gatherings celebrate the changing seasons, completion of work, and continuity of the clan. They also make it possible to arrange marriages, exchange news, settle disputes, and renew alliances.

Additional notes 17

Festivities include great meals, gambling, contests of skill, feats of strength, races, music, and dancing. Festival nights are often noisy, warm, and marked by generous consumption of food and drink.

Additional notes 18

The Earth Cult holds the foremost place in their spirituality. It honors the fertility of soil, stability of the seasons, harvests, and prosperity of the household.

Additional notes 19

In some regions the Cult of Growth is also widespread. It places greater emphasis on germination, birth, renewal, and abundance of the herds.

Additional notes 20

These cults are closely tied to everyday life. Rites may accompany sowing, harvest, the birth of animals, establishment of a new farm, marriages, and seasonal festivals.

Additional notes 21

Gramuz religion does not rest on a powerful clergy. It is transmitted by elders, heads of households, and a few individuals regarded as especially close to natural forces.

Additional notes 22

The rare spell-users most often belong to the Urdharkona, or Urdharkonur in the plural, specialists close to Animists. They act as healers, advisers, interpreters of natural signs, and guardians of tradition.

Additional notes 23

Gramuik is their principal language. Westron is also known, especially in communities near trade routes or in contact with Gondor.

Additional notes 24

Gramuz may also learn Logathig, Eothrik, Atliduk, Nahaiduk, Bethteur, certain forms of Orcish, or Waildyth among travelers, warriors, and scouts.

Additional notes 25

The Gramuz are renowned as independent, determined, and direct. They appreciate people who keep their word, work hard, and defend their interests without evasion.

Additional notes 26

They respect material success when it rests on effort, prudence, and good management. A landowner able to enlarge his fields, improve his herd, or protect his community naturally gains prestige.

Additional notes 27

This appreciation of success can nevertheless produce strong rivalries. Disputes over pasture, boundaries, horses, or marriages can last for several generations when no recognized authority succeeds in settling them.

Additional notes 28

Gramuz chiefly wear linen and wool. Everyday clothing generally includes breeches, a tunic or medium-length shirt, leggings, a cloth cloak, and soft shoes. Women often wear a short tunic or simple dress accompanied by leggings.

Additional notes 29

Additional notes 30

Additional notes 31

Gramuz fight mainly on foot or horseback in small units. They excel at defending farms, skirmishing, ambushes, and battles fought in open terrain.

Additional notes 32

Additional notes 33

Additional notes 35

Additional notes 36

Additional notes 37

The Gramuz are thus a people of landowners, farmers, and herders fiercely attached to their lands. La religion gramuz ne repose pas sur un clergé puissant. Elle est transmise par les anciens, les chefs de famille et quelques individus considérés comme particulièrement proches des forces naturelles.

Les Gramuz sont réputés indépendants, déterminés et directs. Ils apprécient les personnes capables de tenir leur parole, de travailler dur et de défendre leurs intérêts sans détour.

Gramuz

The Gramuz, whose name means “Men of the Plains” in their language, descend from ancient Eriadorians who crossed the Gap of Rohan at the beginning of the Third Age before moving into the vast plains of Rhovanion. They settled chiefly north of Nan Celduin, the valley of the Celduin, in regions of gentle hills, open pasture, and fertile land crossed by many streams. Their culture is profoundly rural, founded on family, clan, animal husbandry, and working the land.

Origins

Gramuz are generally of medium to tall stature, with robust and sometimes stocky builds. Men often reach about six feet and women about five feet four inches. Their complexion is fair, their hair most often blond, and their eyes frequently blue. Their life expectancy generally lies between sixty-five and eighty-five years.

Appearance

Men readily wear beards, which often serve as a sign of maturity, respectability, and family belonging. Hairstyles and clothing remain simple, but prosperous families may use embroidery, brooches, or worked belts to display rank.

Communities

Gramuz society is essentially agrarian. Most families live in small, scattered communities made up of one to three related households. These settlements do not always form true villages: they are more often groups of farms established near a common refuge.

Clans and chiefs

Dwellings resemble the longhouses of other Northmen, but in a shorter form better suited to small family groups. Under a single roof they often bring together family members, stores, and sometimes certain animals during the coldest months.

Family

Each community generally has a defensible place: a hill enclosed by a palisade, an enclosure protected by a ditch, a small fortified mound, or a refuge near a ford or grove. In peacetime these spaces are used mainly to gather domestic animals. In the event of raid or attack, they become the heart of collective defense.

Agriculture and animal husbandry

The Gramuz are organized into clans led by hereditary chiefs. The authority of these leaders rests on lineage, but also on their ability to protect the lands, arbitrate disputes, and redistribute resources during difficult periods.

Festivals

The chief is not an absolute ruler. He must take account of elders, heads of households, and the reputation of the most respected warriors. A decision contrary to the clan's interests may be challenged, especially if it threatens herds, crops, or collective honor.

Religion

The Gramuz are independent and determined. They have difficulty accepting foreign authority when it rests neither on kinship nor on a recognized oath. This independence does not prevent alliances, but they generally demand clear and personal agreements.

Languages

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. A wife usually joins her husband's family and becomes part of his household.

Temperament

Unions may be contracted outside the clan or tribe, but marriages with non-Northern peoples remain rare. This reserve does not necessarily arise from open hostility; it mainly reflects a desire to preserve customs, kinship ties, and community cohesion.

Clothing

The extended family is the fundamental unit of society. Land, herds, tools, and duties pass between generations. An individual who loses his family therefore loses not only relatives, but also his social and economic place.

War

The Gramuz cultivate grain, raise pigs, cattle, sheep, and horses, and exploit the rich lands of the river valleys. Their wealth is measured less in coin than in livestock, land, stores, and reputation.

Relations

The horse holds an important place without dominating their entire culture as it does among the Rohirrim. Gramuz breed sturdy mounts suited to farm work, travel, and war. The most prosperous families often own good breeding stock and can gain considerable prestige from the quality of their animals.

Professions

Trade readily uses Gondorian coinage, but exchange in kind remains common. Animals, tools, grain, cloth, and services can all serve as payment.

Place in character creation

The cycle of the year profoundly structures their life. Four great festivals bring scattered communities together: midsummer, midwinter, the spring equinox, and the autumn equinox.

Additional notes 16

These gatherings celebrate the changing seasons, completion of work, and continuity of the clan. They also make it possible to arrange marriages, exchange news, settle disputes, and renew alliances.

Additional notes 17

Festivities include great meals, gambling, contests of skill, feats of strength, races, music, and dancing. Festival nights are often noisy, warm, and marked by generous consumption of food and drink.

Additional notes 18

The Earth Cult holds the foremost place in their spirituality. It honors the fertility of soil, stability of the seasons, harvests, and prosperity of the household.

Additional notes 19

In some regions the Cult of Growth is also widespread. It places greater emphasis on germination, birth, renewal, and abundance of the herds.

Additional notes 20

These cults are closely tied to everyday life. Rites may accompany sowing, harvest, the birth of animals, establishment of a new farm, marriages, and seasonal festivals.

Additional notes 21

Gramuz religion does not rest on a powerful clergy. It is transmitted by elders, heads of households, and a few individuals regarded as especially close to natural forces.

Additional notes 22

The rare spell-users most often belong to the Urdharkona, or Urdharkonur in the plural, specialists close to Animists. They act as healers, advisers, interpreters of natural signs, and guardians of tradition.

Additional notes 23

Gramuik is their principal language. Westron is also known, especially in communities near trade routes or in contact with Gondor.

Additional notes 24

Gramuz may also learn Logathig, Eothrik, Atliduk, Nahaiduk, Bethteur, certain forms of Orcish, or Waildyth among travelers, warriors, and scouts.

Additional notes 25

The Gramuz are renowned as independent, determined, and direct. They appreciate people who keep their word, work hard, and defend their interests without evasion.

Additional notes 26

They respect material success when it rests on effort, prudence, and good management. A landowner able to enlarge his fields, improve his herd, or protect his community naturally gains prestige.

Additional notes 27

This appreciation of success can nevertheless produce strong rivalries. Disputes over pasture, boundaries, horses, or marriages can last for several generations when no recognized authority succeeds in settling them.

Additional notes 28

Gramuz chiefly wear linen and wool. Everyday clothing generally includes breeches, a tunic or medium-length shirt, leggings, a cloth cloak, and soft shoes. Women often wear a short tunic or simple dress accompanied by leggings.

Additional notes 29

The Gramuz are not an exclusively warrior people, but almost every community must know how to defend itself against raids, Orcs, and wild beasts.

Additional notes 30

Their most common weapons are spear, short bow, longbow, one-handed axe, short sword, and broadsword. Leather is their most frequent protection. Wealthier warriors or men of a chief's retinue may wear mail or scale armor.

Additional notes 31

Gramuz fight mainly on foot or horseback in small units. They excel at defending farms, skirmishing, ambushes, and battles fought in open terrain.

Additional notes 32

They hate Orcs, whom they regard as raiders, murderers, and natural enemies of their communities. Relations with other Northmen vary. They may trade, ally, or quarrel with Woodmen, Éothéod, Rohirrim, or urban communities of Rhovanion.

Additional notes 33

They also maintain economic relations with Gondor, whose coins circulate in their lands. Some clans welcome this influence; others fear that it may weaken their independence.

Additional notes 34

Gramuz may follow almost every profession except Barbarian and professions specific to other races or cultures. Spell-users remain rare, and the natural traditions of the Urdharkona are the most common among them.

Additional notes 35

Their training favors driving and caring for animals, animal husbandry, agriculture, plains survival, weather watching, tracking, foraging, cooking, leatherworking and woodworking, hunting and war weapons, dance, and community festivities.

Additional notes 36

This Culture is particularly suitable for characters from an isolated farm in Rhovanion, a herding clan, a fortified agricultural community, a family of landowners, the retinue of a local chief, a group of herd guards, or a line of horse traders.

Additional notes 37

The Gramuz are thus a people of landowners, farmers, and herders fiercely attached to their lands. Their strength comes neither from great cities nor from standing armies, but from family cohesion, knowledge of the plains, and determination to preserve the farms and herds upon which their whole existence depends.
